narrative:
The model estimated a 78% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure more likely than success by a wide margin, so your law school application was denied because the review treated that risk as too high.

The strongest reason was your Year 3 class standing: you were in the first decile, far below the average accepted student’s fifth-to-sixth decile range, and this pushed the decision most strongly toward likely bar failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most influential factor; it is well below the accepted-student average of about 37 and also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.10 was the third most important factor, though in this particular prediction its influence leaned toward passing rather than failure; even so, it was not enough to offset the other two signals. Your part-time status and middle-income background were not among the leading reasons.

To improve your chances, focus on the two strongest concerns. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, and provide evidence of stronger upper-level academic performance or additional coursework if available. Ask admissions whether you can submit updated scores or grades, discuss any mitigating circumstances, and seek feedback on whether a later application or conditional pathway is realistic.
